GraceTechnology.ArchitectureStatus: Target architecture is selected for direct implementation; exact toolchain versions and cryptographic crate choices remain pending review and device compatibility work.

PortableRustCore.Language: Rust shared by the Wear OS native library and Windows receiver.
PortableRustCore.Responsibilities: Versioned wire types, recording manifests, bounded chunk streaming, hashing, transfer state, checkpoint negotiation, idempotent request handling, cancellation, and protocol compatibility.
PortableRustCore.Boundary: Rust is a cancellable component invoked by Kotlin on Wear OS and owns the receiver service on Windows. It does not become a permanent autonomous watch daemon.
PortableRustCore.Interface: Expose a narrow versioned FFI surface for file-descriptor reads, selected-network identity, cancellation, progress, and terminal outcomes.
Expose a versioned HTTPS session contract for status, transfer creation, durable range query, chunk upload, completion, and abort.

WearOsPlatform.Ui: Compose for Wear OS with circular-screen layouts and explicit manual session controls.
WearOsPlatform.Ownership: Kotlin owns Android lifecycle, permissions, MediaStore or SAF access, file descriptors, Wi-Fi Network acquisition, notifications, foreground or scheduled work, and energy eligibility.
WearOsPlatform.NativeBridge: Android NDK loads the shared Rust core as a cdylib through a narrow JNI adapter; no Kotlin aggregate state may claim native transfer success before an owner result.
WearOsPlatform.Scheduling: Use supported user-initiated foreground or OS-cooperative job facilities. Do not add a persistent watch polling engine.

WindowsReceiver.Runtime: Tokio for bounded asynchronous work and Axum or an equivalent reviewed HTTP server for the authenticated receiver surface.
WindowsReceiver.Storage: SQLite or an equivalent durable registry records transfer identity, chunk ranges, checkpoints, final fingerprint, and commit state.
WindowsReceiver.Ownership: The Rust receiver owns disk correctness, atomic finalization, resource limits, and recovery when the Kotlin desktop UI is closed.
WindowsReceiver.Network: Bind only to an explicit private-network listener and document the Windows Firewall rule and listen address.

DesktopUi.Ownership: The desktop UI owns presentation, pairing actions, destination selection, settings, history, and diagnostics. It consumes receiver-owned projections and cannot fabricate durable transfer state.
DesktopUi.Lifecycle: Service autostart and tray behavior are user-configurable; the receiver remains correct when the main window is closed.

ProtocolBoundaries.Versioning: Wire protocol, FFI surface, manifest schema, and durable registry migrations are versioned independently and reject incompatible versions before transfer.
ProtocolBoundaries.Streaming: Audio is streamed from a descriptor through bounded buffers; whole-file JVM or Rust heap buffering is prohibited.
ProtocolBoundaries.Hashing: Each chunk has a defined digest and the receiver stores a full final fingerprint after manifest and range validation. The algorithm and compatibility policy are fixed in a future security review.
ProtocolBoundaries.NetworkBinding: Android Kotlin selects the Wi-Fi Network and passes its identity or a bound socket to Rust; a connected Bluetooth route is never treated as payload transport.
ProtocolBoundaries.Cancellation: Cancellation tokens cross the Kotlin-to-Rust boundary and terminal cleanup is idempotent.

PlatformKeystores.Wear: Watch identity material and receiver pins use Android-protected storage.
PlatformKeystores.Windows: Receiver identity keys and pairing records use Windows-protected storage appropriate to the packaged application.
PlatformKeystores.Rule: Secrets never appear in source, test fixtures, ordinary logs, or public repository artifacts.

ToolchainAndTesting.Build: Future implementation changes will establish the Rust workspace, Android NDK/JNI build, Wear APK, Windows receiver package, and Compose Desktop package in their own approved scope.
ToolchainAndTesting.Categories: Rust unit and property tests; cross-language protocol tests; JNI and Kotlin lifecycle tests; Windows receiver integration tests; security tests; network interruption and corruption tests; physical Wear OS, hotspot, battery, thermal, and packaging gates.
ToolchainAndTesting.Evidence: Local compilation and deterministic tests establish code contracts only. Samsung file access, hotspot forwarding, Wi-Fi binding on the target firmware, and overnight energy behavior require physical-device evidence.

DeferredChoices.Choice: Minimum Wear OS and Android versions and exact packaging/distribution targets.
Reviewed PAKE and TLS crate selection, key rotation, and revocation storage policy.
Chunk size, concurrency, session deadline, and throughput budgets after measured hardware trials.
